title: Halloween
wiki_lead:
Halloween, also known as All Hallows' Eve or All Saints' Eve,  is a celebration observed in many countries  on 31 October, the eve of Western Christianity's feast of All Hallows' Day. It is at the beginning of the observance of Allhallowtide, the time in the Christian liturgical year dedicated to remembering the dead, including saints (hallows), Christian martyrs, and all the faithful departed. In popular culture, Halloween has become a celebration of horror and is associated with the macabre and the supernatural.
One theory holds that many Halloween traditions were influenced by Celtic harvest festivals, particularly the Gaelic festival Samhain, which is believed to have pagan roots. Some theories go further and suggest that Samhain may have been Christianized as All Hallows' Day, along with its eve, by the Christian Church. Other scholars say Halloween began independently as a Christian holiday, being the vigil of All Hallows' Day. Celebrated in Ireland and Scotland for centuries, Irish and Scottish immigrants brought many Halloween customs to North America in the 19th century. Through American influence, various Halloween customs spread to other countries by the late 20th and early 21st centuries.
Popular Halloween activities include trick-or-treating (or the related guising and souling), attending Halloween costume parties, carving pumpkins or turnips into jack-o'-lanterns, lighting bonfires, apple bobbing, divination games, playing pranks, visiting haunted attractions, telling frightening stories, and watching horror or Halloween-themed films. Some Christians practice the observances of All Hallows' Eve, including attending church services and lighting candles on the graves of the dead, although it is a secular celebration for others. Historically, some Christians abstained from meat on All Hallows' Eve, a tradition reflected in the eating of certain vegetarian foods on this day, including apples, potato pancakes, and soul cakes.

Etymology

Hallow derives from Middle English halowen, from Old English hālig which means holy; it has been used synonymously with the word saint. The word Halloween or Hallowe'en comes from the Lowland Scots form of All Hallows' Eve (the evening before All Hallows' Day): even is the Scots term for 'eve' or 'evening', and is contracted to e'en or een; so (All) Hallow(s) E(v)en became Halloween. A term equivalent to 'All Hallows Eve' as attested in Old English. Thus, the name originates in Christianity, and means "Saints' eve(ning)".


History


Christian origins and historical customs

'Halloween' comes from All Hallows' Eve, being the night before All Hallows' Day (All Saints' Day), which is followed by All Souls' Day on 2 November. These three days are a part of Allhallowtide, a time when Western Christians honour all Christian martyrs and saints, as well as pray for departed souls. Halloween is influenced by Christian beliefs and practices surrounding these holy days. Christian holidays such as Christmas and Easter have vigils that begin the night before, as does All Hallows. 
After the persecution of Christians in the Roman Empire, "there were more martyrs than there were days in the year, and so one day was set apart in honor of them all, and called All Saints' Day." Commemorations of all saints and martyrs were held by several churches on various dates, mostly in springtime. In 4th-century Roman Edessa it was held on 13 May, and that date was endorsed by Pope Boniface IV in 609, when he re-dedicated the Pantheon in Rome to Mary and all martyrs. This was the date of Lemuria, an ancient Roman festival of the dead, when it was believed that restless and vengeful souls wandered. Some folklorists also suggest the ancient Roman festival of Parentalia (including Feralia) influenced All Saints' and All Souls' days. grok_lead: Halloween is an annual holiday celebrated on October 31, primarily in countries of the Western world such as the United States, Canada, Ireland, and the United Kingdom, featuring activities like costume-wearing, trick-or-treating, carving jack-o'-lanterns, and hosting parties with games and seasonal treats. The holiday's roots trace back over 2,000 years to the ancient Celtic festival of Samhain (pronounced "SAH-win"), observed by the Celts in what is now Ireland, the United Kingdom, and northern France to mark the end of the harvest season and the onset of winter, which was seen as a time when the boundary between the living world and the spirit realm thinned, allowing ghosts and fairies to roam freely. During Samhain, Celts lit bonfires to honor the harvest and ward off evil spirits, while later accounts describe participants wearing costumes or disguisesâoften animal skins or masksâto blend in with or frighten away wandering souls, though direct evidence for this as an ancient Celtic practice is limited. Communities also left food offerings outside homes for these spirits, a practice that foreshadowed later traditions like trick-or-treating. In the 8th century, Christian missionaries influenced the festival by designating November 1 as All Saints' Day (also known as All Hallows' Day) to honor saints and martyrs, shifting the focus from pagan rituals to Christian reverence while retaining many Samhain customs on the preceding evening, which became known as All Hallows' Eve or Halloween. This blending incorporated elements like the Roman festival of Pomona ( goddess of fruit and seeds), which contributed traditions such as bobbing for apples, symbolizing fertility and harvest. By the 9th century, the holiday had spread across Europe, with practices like "guising"âchildren dressing up and begging for treatsâemerging in Scotland and Ireland as early as the 16th century to commemorate the souls in purgatory. Halloween evolved further with Irish and Scottish immigrants bringing traditions to North America in the mid-19th century, where the pumpkin ânative to the Americasâreplaced turnips for carving jack-o'-lanterns, inspired by the Irish legend of Stingy Jack, a man doomed to wander with a lantern made from a carved vegetable. In the United States, the holiday gained popularity in the late 19th and early 20th centuries through community events and school activities, but trick-or-treating as a widespread custom surged in the 1940s and 1950s amid post-World War II suburban growth and increased candy production, transforming Halloween into a commercialized celebration of fun, fright, and fall festivities. Today, it emphasizes secular entertainment while echoing its ancient themes of harvest, the supernatural, and communal bonding.
